and dividing by [𝔼(Gt)]2=R¯2(1+2cw/m)+O(m−2) gives a relative variance of vR/R¯2+[A+(R¯2+vR)cw]/(R¯2m) to first order in 1/m, which is Eq. (15).

B. Extensions

B.1. Precision of the environmental variance

Proposition 4 (Precision of environmental variance). Suppose that R1,…,RT are independent gamma variables with known mean R¯ and variance vR, and let ξ=R¯2/vR. Any unbiased estimator of vR based on the counts from the T periods has relative standard error at least

(B.1)

where ψ′ is the trigamma function. As ξ→∞, the bound tends to the Gaussian value 2/T.

Proof. The counts depend on vR only through R1:T, so by the data processing inequality the Fisher information for vR in the counts cannot exceed that in R1:T. With the mean fixed, the gamma shape is ξ and the scale is vR/R¯. The information for ξ in one observation is ψ′(ξ)−1/ξ, and dξ/dvR=−ξ/vR, so the information for vR in T periods is Tξ(ξψ′(ξ)−1)/vR2. The Cramér–Rao inequality gives Eq. (B.1). The limit follows from ψ′(ξ)=1/ξ+1/(2ξ2)+O(ξ−3).

□

At the baseline of Table S7 (R¯=1.15, vR=0.04), ξ=33.06 and ξ(ξψ′(ξ)−1)=0.505, so the relative standard error is at least 0.812 with 3 periods, 0.445 with 10 periods and 0.199 with 50 periods. The constant 0.505 is specific to this baseline, and Eq. (B.1) is the general form.

B.2. Budget threshold with autocorrelated environments

With autocorrelation ϕ, the environmental term of Proposition 3 is vRe(T) with e(T)=S(ϕ,T)/T2. Define gT=−T2e′(T), treating T as continuous, so that gT=1 for independent periods, and let m0*=(c0/c1)m× be the optimum of Eq. (8).

Proposition 5 (Budget threshold). Under the budget constraint ℬ=T(c0+c1m), the optimal case volume per period satisfies m*=m0*(gT*)−1/2, where T* is the optimal number of periods. If gT increases in T from g1<1 towards (1+ϕ)/(1−ϕ)>1, there is a unique T† with gT†=1, and m* exceeds m0* when T*<T† and falls below it when T*>T†. The two regimes meet at the budget

(B.2)

which is expressed in units of the cost per reported case when c1=1.

Proof. Writing the sampling term as Ac1/(ℬ−c0T) and differentiating vRe(T)+Ac1/(ℬ−c0T) with respect to T gives the first-order condition vRgT=c0A/(c1m2), so m*2=m0*2/gT*. The ordering of m* and m0* follows from the monotonicity of gT, and at T*=T† the budget constraint gives Eq. (B.2).

□

For ϕ=0.8, gT increases in T and T†=4.484. With c0/c1=100 and the baseline balance scale, m0*=72.86 and ℬ†=775.0; over the uncorrected scenario range of 21.3 to 49.2 cases per generation in Section 6.3, ℬ† ranges from 655.3 to 762.9 (762.85 rounded, Table S7). The calculation treats T as continuous and the environmental process as stationary, so it applies within a season and not across seasons with different mean transmission.

B.3. Between-season variance

Corollary 2 (Season-level bound). Suppose that season effects η1,…,ηS are independent Gaussian variables with unknown mean and variance vS, and that the counts depend on vS only through the season effects. Any unbiased estimator of vS based on the counts has relative standard error at least 2/(S−1), which is 1.00 for S=3 and 0.816 for S=4.

Proof. Let δ be an unbiased estimator based on the counts. Because the conditional distribution of the counts given η1:S does not depend on the unknown parameters (μ,vS) and unbiasedness holds for all (μ,vS), 𝔼(δ∣η1:S) is a function of the season effects that is unbiased for vS, and its variance does not exceed that of δ. The sample mean and sample variance of η1:S are complete and sufficient, so the sample variance is the minimum-variance unbiased estimator of vS, with variance 2vS2/(S−1) (Lehmann and Casella, 1998; Lehmann and Romano, 2005; Searle et al., 1992).

□

The bound uses S−1 degrees of freedom because the mean across seasons is estimated; the corresponding bound with a known mean, 2/S, is smaller (Table S7). Season-specific intercepts for three and four seasons are reported separately in Table S5.

B.4. Testing whether transmission exceeds one

For R>R′, the likelihood ratio of Eq. (2) increases in c because R/(k+ρR) increases in R, so the family has a monotone likelihood ratio in Ct. The test that rejects Rt≤1 when Ct≥cα therefore has a power function that does not decrease in Rt, and by the Karlin–Rubin theorem it is uniformly most powerful at its attained level α*=PRt=1(Ct≥cα)≤α (Karlin and Rubin, 1956; Lehmann and Romano, 2005). Because Ct is discrete, α* is generally below the nominal level; optimality holds at α*, not at α, unless the test is randomised or a mid-p value is used.

B.5. Shrinkage as an ideal bound

Part (iv) of Proposition 1 excludes estimators that are biased given Rt. Consider θ̂λ=(1−λ)R̂t+λμ0 for a fixed benchmark μ0 with Δ=μ0−R¯. Its mean squared error for R¯ is given by:

(B.3)

where V is given by Eq. (4). The minimum is at λ*=V/(V+Δ2), where MSE(λ*)=VΔ2/(V+Δ2), which is below vR if and only if Δ2<vR(1+m/m×). The weight λ* depends on the unknown R¯ and V, so this is an ideal bound and not a feasible estimator; an empirical Bayes or hierarchical estimator estimates the weight from the data and does not attain it (Stoner et al., 2019).

Each setting changes one element of the data-matched design (Section 6.8); the analyst’s generation interval stays at a mean of 3.6 days throughout. Intervals combine 2000 joint two-way bootstrap draws of the two empirical intercepts with draws of the calibration line from its Monte Carlo sampling distribution. κ=𝔼(â)/(vR/R¯2) at the grid value of vR nearest to the implied variance. Agree marks settings in which the 95% interval of the difference between the two implied variances contains zero; the generic design of the first simulation is shown as a bridge and is not counted among the ten settings.

r1 is the pooled lag-1 autocorrelation of the relative deviation x/x¯block−1 within state-season blocks. The interval for the data comes from a state-cluster bootstrap with 1000 draws; simulated rows give the mean and the 2.5% to 97.5% range of r1 over panels at vR=0.04 (200 panels per value of vR for the added settings, 100 for the others), and Data pct. is the percentile of the empirical value in that distribution. The analyst’s generation interval stays at a mean of 3.6 days; 2.9 and 4.3 days are the ends of the 95% interval for the serial interval of influenza in Cowling et al. (2009). Overdispersed admissions use a gamma–Poisson mixture on weekly counts.
